meta.title: Zetta: bots that work on your server while you do something else
meta.description: Zetta is an open source, self-hosted workspace for bots. Ask your chief for an outcome. Come back to results, or to the one thing that needs you.

hero.eyebrow: Free, open source, runs on your server
hero.lead: Zetta is an open source web app that you host yourself. Give your personal chief a job, such as a weekly brief or a pull request review. It hands the work to specialist bots on your server, and you come back to the result, or to the one question it cannot answer alone.
hero.installLabel: One line on macOS, Linux or WSL
hero.note: Bots run the coding agents installed on your server: Pi, Codex, OMP, Claude Code, OpenCode and Cursor.
hero.robotAlt: The Zetta robot at the center of a graph. Four bots are connected to it and to each other, and a line runs from the robot to a cloud connected to GitHub, Notion, Cloudflare, Sentry and Linear. One bot waits for you. Illustration.

live.lead: A real recording of the app, with demo data. The chief takes a brief, designs a small team of bots and asks you to approve each step.
live.note: Zetta in light mode, with demo data. Waiting time is sped up.
live.videoLabel: A recording of the Zetta app in light mode: the chief designs a team of bots from a brief, and each step waits for approval. Demo data.

features.lead: Routines, memory, tasks, a browser and a desktop. Every clip below is the real app, with demo data.

tiles.title: Work that starts without you
tiles.body: Schedule a briefing, a newsletter or a review queue to run on its own. The agenda syncs both ways with the main calendar of each Google account you connect.
tiles.alt: The routines page: a morning briefing, a Friday newsletter and a pull request queue, each with its next run. Demo data.

tiles.title: What matters stays
tiles.body: Bots keep what matters between chats. Company knowledge is searchable, even with a local embedding model.
tiles.alt: Three notes a bot keeps in memory. Illustration.

tiles.title: A desktop on your server
tiles.body: Bots can use a Linux desktop on your server. You set limits on memory, CPU and how many run at once.
tiles.alt: A recording of a bot using a computer and a terminal in the Zetta dashboard. Demo data.

tiles.title: A person takes over at the sign-in
tiles.body: Bots can use a browser. At a sign-in, a person takes over and the bot carries on after.
tiles.alt: A recording of a bot reading pages in a browser and asking a person to sign in. Demo data.

tiles.title: They ask only when they need you
tiles.body: The Inbox lists what is working, what is blocked and what has a new result.
tiles.alt: The Inbox lists two items that need you: send the newsletter to the whole team list, and a blocked GitHub login. Demo data.

tiles.title: Who has what, and what is stuck
tiles.body: Tasks move from backlog to in progress, blocked, review and done. Each card shows the bot that owns it.
tiles.alt: The task board with columns backlog, in progress, blocked and review, each card showing its bot. Demo data.

tiles.title: One chat for each intention
tiles.body: Each bot keeps many chats, so the context stays clean and you can find the work later. Rooms put several bots and people in one conversation.
tiles.alt: A chat with the Writer bot. The newsletter draft ends with a question that waits for approval. Demo data.

engines.lead: Everything below exists in the repository today. Each bot can run on a different agent.

groups.title: Connected apps
groups.body: Connect the accounts your bots need from Studio. Sharing a bot never shares your credentials.

groups.title: Your coding tools
groups.body: Claude Code or Cursor can work as a member of your team through a built-in connection, with the same permission checks as the web app.

groups.title: Messaging
groups.body: Telegram with your own bot token, and WhatsApp through your own WAHA server.

chief.lead: Zetta is the chief of your bots. It hires them, hands out the work, keeps the routines running and brings you only what needs you. It proposes, and you decide.

points.title: Ask for an outcome
points.body: No configuration screens to learn first. Say what you want done.

points.title: Every write is an Approve card
points.body: The chief proposes a bot, a routine or a task. Nothing is created until you approve it.

points.title: Secrets stay out of the chat
points.body: When a bot needs a password or a key, the chief opens a form. The secret never goes through the conversation.

chief.alt: A chat with the chief. The person asks for a weekly summary of their repositories, and the chief proposes a Researcher bot with an Approve button. Illustration.
chief.ask: Every Monday, summarize what changed in our repositories and send me a brief.
chief.reply: I can set that up. I would add one bot for it:

fields.label: First task
fields.value: Summarize last week's merged pull requests

chief.orgAlt: The Zetta robot at the top, as the chief, with four bots below it: Writer and Researcher are working, Reviewer is done, and Editor needs you. Illustration.
chief.capsTitle: What the chief manages for you

caps.title: Hire a bot
caps.body: Describe the role. The chief proposes the agent, the access and the first task.

caps.title: Build a team from one brief
caps.body: A brief becomes several bots, each with its own job.

caps.title: Schedule routines
caps.body: Briefings and reviews that run on their own, when you say.

caps.title: Add skills, plugins and MCP servers
caps.body: Give a bot the tools it needs, from the skills library to your connected apps.

caps.title: Open a room
caps.body: Put several bots and people in one conversation.

caps.title: Take secrets through a form
caps.body: Passwords and keys go into a private form, never into the chat.

install.lead: You need Git, OpenSSL and a running Docker or Podman. Zetta starts a web app, an API and a Postgres database.
install.note: Free under the MIT license. It is early: read the repository and its issues before you depend on it.

steps.title: Run the installer
steps.body: On macOS, Linux or WSL. It clones the repository, writes the two .env files with fresh secrets and starts the containers. Run it again to update.

steps.title: Finish setup in the browser
steps.body: Open http://localhost:3001 and paste the setup key from apps/server/.env. You become the admin of this install.

steps.title: Ask your chief for something
steps.body: Describe a job in the chat. The chief proposes the bots, and you approve them.

manual.summary: Prefer to do it by hand?
manual.body: These are the same steps the installer runs. The full list of settings is in apps/server/.env.schema.

items.a: Yes. It is open source under the MIT license. You pay for your own server and for the agents you run on it, and nothing to Zetta.
On your server. Zetta starts a web app, an API and a Postgres database there, and your chats, tasks and memory stay in that database.
Zetta has no model bill of its own. Each bot runs one of the agents installed on your server (Pi, Codex, OMP, Claude Code, OpenCode or Cursor), signed in the way that agent normally signs in.
Deleting files, administrator commands and sending mail. The chief's changes are Approve cards too. Ordinary actions run on their own, and a blocked or uncertain result always comes back to you.

items.q: Can I use it from my phone?
items.a: You can message your bots from Telegram with your own bot token, or from WhatsApp through your own WAHA server. Sending from WhatsApp stays off until you turn it on.

items.q: Which systems does it run on?
items.a: The installer supports macOS, Linux and WSL, and needs Git, OpenSSL and a running Docker or Podman. On Windows, run it inside WSL.

cta.lead: One command on a server you control. Open source, MIT.
